PONTSHO MOHLANKA – THE MURDEROUS NEIGHBOUR

By: Ntokozo Miya | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Two years after the ritual murder of three Orange Farm children, their killer is in jail, but are women & children any safer - and has the conviction restored this community's faith in the police?

Unique Selling Point:
With child-killer Pontsho Mohlanka behind bars for life, the families of her little victims provide insight into how their friendly neighbour morphed into a monster to whom prosperity was more important than human life.

Summary:
On the morning of the 15th of April 2020, 5-year-old Mzwandile Zitho from Orange Farm, south of Joburg, disappeared. The community joined his family in their search for the boy. His grandmother Nompumelelo reported his disappearance to the police, but on her return, neighbours confirmed her worst fears – Mzwandile was dead. He hadn’t strayed far - his body was found nearby, in a shebeen that the owner operated with his girlfriend, Pontsho Mohlanka.
When Gogo Nompumelelo saw her grandson's corpse, she could scarcely believe her eyes. He was in an upright position, propped between a fridge and a counter inside the shebeen. There were strings around his neck and ankles, and a slimy black substance smeared on his body.
As the occupants of the building where the body was found, Pontsho and her boyfriend were arrested on suspicion of murder. The boyfriend was released due to a lack of evidence, but Pontsho remained in custody, only to be released five months later when the charges against her were temporarily withdrawn, pending a toxicology report.
Three days after her release, two more children went missing. In a scene eerily similar to the one months earlier, the bodies of Simphiwe Mgcina, 6, and Mpho Makondo, 8, were found near the shebeen, also covered in a black substance.
Pontsho was rearrested. As the investigation unfolded, her boyfriend was placed in witness protection and would later testify against Pontsho. During the trial, he said she had killed the children as part of a prosperity ritual, meant to grow their tavern business. Pontsho pointed the finger at him, claiming that he was the one behind the rituals, but she failed to convince the courts.
Following a month-long trial, Pontsho was found guilty of all three murders in August 2022 and will be sentenced on the 13th of September.

Further information:
Orange Farm is a community plagued by violence against women and children, so much so that it has been allocated a Green Door ’safe place’ - where survivors of violence can find refuge - and their cases expedited. But residents are sceptical - they have for too long watched criminals operating without fear of the police, whom everyone believes are ineffectual. After all, they say, if the police had properly investigated Mzwandile’s murder, Pontsho’s last two victims would not have died.
There are also concerns that Pontsho may not have been working alone, but acting on advice that human sacrifice would equate to prosperity. They have no faith that police will follow up and arrest others involved and doubt that ’safe places’ will change the police’s woeful investigative abilities.
Whatever the various motives behind the crimes, the community believes that perpetrators commit these crimes freely, confident that the cops won't connect them. Residents also complain about a lack of visible policing in the area, despite the recent allocation of 15 additional vehicles.
By focusing on this case, we will tell the story of Orange Farm’s crime scourge and why we report on the same horrific incidents, year after year and find out whether the latest initiative has any chance of success.

Script:


FOR FINAL MIX - MURDEROUS NEIGHBOUR

NATSOUND – driving shots of Orange Farm
INTRO – Orange Farm… one of Johannesburg’s newest townships, home to around four hundred thousand families.

A rapid influx of people, without the services to match, has seen it grapple with unemployment, drug abuse, and crime.

Yet nothing could have prepared this already struggling community for the killings of three young children 2 years ago, the gruesome details of which emerged in a recently ended trial.
BREATHER – and then fade to black
NATSOUND – start sequence, wind blowing as Gogo Zitho walks in cemetery
VO – Some people avoid cemeteries…but for Gogo Nompumelelo Zitho it’s sacred ground.. to connect with the people she's lost. And yet she never thought she’d have to visit her grandson Mzwandile here.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER

I miss you, my child. I will always love you.
VO – What's made dealing with his death harder, is that he was killed by someone she considered a friendly neighbour.
BREATHER
LINK - FX3_0917 – One minute 5-year-old Mzwandile was playing in this yard at his home in Orange Farm in the south of Johannesburg, the next, he was gone. Hours later, he was found dead in the house literally right across the street.
BREATHER
VO – One morning in April 2020, Gogo Zitho called Mzwandile…Wandi, to come and eat.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER

When I looked for him around 11am, I couldn't find him anywhere, even the places he'd normally go to.
VO – Police joined her initial search, but they couldn't find him. She filed a missing person's report at the station.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER

When I got back from the police station around 6pm, I found a lot of people outside. They told me that Wandi had been found. He was at the tavern.
VO – Gogo Zitho knew the couple who ran the tavern across the road very well... but she was stopped from entering before police arrived.
Crime scene officers discovered a bizarre scene.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER

He was propped in an upright position between a fridge and a counter. There was a rope, a key and a bottle with muthi on the fridge nearby.
CLAIRE – All of this shocked you?
A lot. The man would sometimes take Mzwandile with him when he went to the mall. Pontsho was always very quiet.
BREATHER
VO – Pontsho Mohlanka was the tavern owner’s girlfriend. They were often seen around… shopping at the spaza… running errands.
Pontsho is a mother herself… to a little boy.
BREATHER
VO – The couple were arrested. The boyfriend later turned state witness and was released. After being detained for five months, Pontsho was released on bail. As the investigation dragged on, she returned to Orange Farm.
MORGINAH MALATJI – MPHO'S GRANDMOTHER

Then two days after her release, she took our children.
BREATHER
VO – Morginah Malatji lived about 500m from the tavern with her 8-year-old granddaughter, Mpho.﻿
MORGINAH MALATJI – MPHO'S GRANDMOTHER

Everyone loved her.
VO – Two doors down, Mpho's best friend Simphiwe - or Panki as he was known - lived with his mom, Busisiwe Mgcina. He was 6.
BUSISIWE MGCINA – SIMPHIWE'S MOTHER – FC PROJECT

Simphiwe was a shy child. If you greeted on the street and tried to play with him, he'd just run away.
VO – In mid-September, a mere 5 months after little Mzwandile's murder, Mpho and Simpiwe also disappeared.
BUSISIWE MGCINA – SIMPHIWE'S MOTHER – FC PROJECT

The police did not treat us well. A lot of time passed before they helped to us.
VO – They searched throughout the night. The next day brought painful news.
BREATHER
MORGINAH MALATJI – MPHO'S GRANDMOTHER

Panki was found in the yard of a house opposite the tavern. Mpho was thrown on the street a few meters away. They were naked.
BREATHER
BUSISIWE MGCINA – SIMPHIWE'S MOTHER – FC PROJECT

I thought Panki was sleeping or he was tired. I didn't think he was dead. When I tried to hold him, an officer told me not to touch him. I almost lost my mind.
BREATHER

VO – The murders sparked fears that a syndicate may be targeting children in Orange Farm. The police, though, had just one suspect in mind.
LINK - FX3_0897 – In July this year, Pontsho Mohlanka stood trial for the 2020 murders. The victims' families demanded justice but above anything else, they wanted to know why their children were killed? Nothing could have prepared them for the answers.
VO – Pontsho gave shocking testimony about dark rituals she claimed were led by her boyfriend's traditional healer.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER – FC PROJECT

She went there to be cleansed of bad luck, after she was arrested for Wandi's murder.
VO – Pontsho testified that Mzwandile was killed during a ritual to grow the tavern's profits. (PAUSE)

Getting caught and arrested meant that something had gone wrong and she needed to be cleansed.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER – FC PROJECT

Her boyfriend told her that they needed to sacrifice two more children, because things weren't going well for them.
VO – By cruel coincidence, the victims of the sacrifice came knocking.
MORGINAH MALATJI – MPHO'S GRANDMOTHER

She heard someone at the door while consulting the healer, and then the children walked into the room.
VO – Those children were Mpho and Panki.
BREATHER
VO – Pontsho claimed to have left the room before the children were killed, and phone records later showed that her boyfriend wasn’t at the scene of the murders. In August, Pontsho was found guilty of suffocating all three children.
MORGINAH MALATJI – MPHO'S GRANDMOTHER

Pontsho really hurt me. I will not heal from this.
BIANCA VAN ASWEGEN – MISSING CHILDREN SA

This is something that we have seen on the increase, especially in Limpopo area, we've had a few cases reported in Orange Farm area, KZN area.
VO - Bianca van Aswegen is from the NGO, Missing Children SA. Their research suggests that 23% of missing children are never found - they’re either trafficked or killed. She says no one knows exactly how many disappearances result in ritual killings.
BIANCA VAN ASWEGEN – MISSING CHILDREN SA

We've still got 2 little boys that have been missing, once since 2013 and another in 2019, that are still missing in the Orange Farm area.
BREATHER
VO - After the verdict, the criminal trial adjourned ahead of sentencing. But there was no break from the criminal onslaught in Orange Farm… where policing leaves much to be desired.
LINDA NDEBELE – COMMUNITY IN ACTION

You see that place, that police station, it's a motel because they are not doing anything. They find them sleeping there.
VO – And he's not joking, this picture of a dozing SAPS member was captured by a local resident.
UPSOUND – start sequence of group meeting and patrolling during shoot day.
VO – Because police have let them down so often when people go missing, residents are used to starting searches themselves. Linda Ndebele is often among them.
LINDA NDEBELE – COMMUNITY IN ACTION

We blow the whistle and then the other members of the community will come and then we gather in one place, and we go and look for that, or whatever that is happening in our area.
UPSOUND - more patrol action
LINK - FX3_0999 - Residents have told us that it's near impossible to get through to the Orange Farm police station by phone. If our experience is anything to go by, they are probably right. In the last week, we've tried to call them ten times with no luck. But ever the optimist, I'm going to try again. [dials, phone rings, after a while Claire says...] Imagine if I'm going through an emergency and this is what I'm met with. [phone rings until it goes to voicemail] 'please try again later...' Orange Farm SAPS meeting our very low expectations of them.
BREATHER
VO – The SAPS communications office later informed us, “The station previously had a challenge with the landlines but it has been resolved…” and… “internal disciplinary steps were instituted” against the napping officers.

They say that policing is taken seriously in Orange Farm and constructive engagements with residents have yielded lower crime levels and a higher crime detection rate.
BREATHER
NATSOUND – chanting/singing outside court. “Pontsho must die in jail. She must die.”
VO – Pontsho's day of reckoning finally arrived on the 13th of September.
NATSOUND – Pontsho walks into court.
VO – Judge Lillian van Wyk at the Palm Ridge court recapped the children's suffering.
JUDGE LILLIAN VAN WYK – HIGH COURT SITTING IN PALM RIDGE

During suffocation, death does not occur immediately. This takes time, however short, in which the accused had time to reflect on her actions.
VO – The judge handed down her sentence.
JUDGE LILLIAN VAN WYK – HIGH COURT SITTING IN PALM RIDGE – FC PROJECT

This court cannot find substantial and compelling circumstances to justify a sentence less than life imprisonment. Count one, life imprisonment. Count two, life imprisonment. Count three, life imprisonment. [Cheers]
LINK - FX3_1002 – The sentence may be harsh and deserved but grieving families say until they know the whole truth about what happened to their children, justice and closure remain elusive.
VO – Though police say there is no evidence of a syndicate targeting children in the area, families refuse to believe that Pontsho acted alone.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER

I am not okay because I have other children. The people that Pontsho worked with will go on to kill more children.
OUTRO – end with cemetery shots.
PROMO 1 – 11 sec
VO – Child disappearances, evil rituals, and a murderous neighbour – we investigate a series of bizarre killings that shook families in the south of Johannesburg.

PROMO 2 – 21 sec
VO – A young boy dies under strange circumstances but the suspect is released just months later...
MORGINAH MALATJI – MPHO'S GRANDMOTHER – Then two days after her release, she took our children.
VO – Families recall chilling testimony about why their childern were taken.
NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER – They would need to sacrifice two more children, because things weren't going well for them.

PROMO 3 – 21 sec
VO – Dark rituals and profits - at the heart of a series of child murders...
BUSISIWE MGCINA – SIMPHIWE'S MOTHER – The police did not treat us well. A lot of time passed before they helped us.
VO – Despite devastating testimonies in court, residents say the area is not cursed, and blame poor policing for rampant crime.
LINDA NDEBELE – COMMUNITY IN ACTION – That police station, it's a motel because they are not doing anything.

If our experience is anything to go by, they are probably right. In the last week, we've tried to call them ten times with no luck. But ever the optimist, I'm going to try again. [dials, phone rings, after a while Claire says...] Imagine if I'm going through an emergency and this is what I'm met with. [phone rings until it goes to voicemail] 'please try again later...' Orange Farm SAPS meeting our very low expectations of them. BREATHER VO – The SAPS communications office later informed us, “The station previously had a challenge with the landlines but it has been resolved…” and… “internal disciplinary steps were instituted” against the napping officers. They say that policing is taken seriously in Orange Farm and constructive engagements with residents have yielded lower crime levels and a higher crime detection rate. BREATHER NATSOUND – chanting/singing outside court. “Pontsho must die in jail. She must die.” VO – Pontsho's day of reckoning finally arrived on the 13th of September. NATSOUND – Pontsho walks into court. VO – Judge Lillian van Wyk at the Palm Ridge court recapped the children's suffering. JUDGE LILLIAN VAN WYK – HIGH COURT SITTING IN PALM RIDGE During suffocation, death does not occur immediately. This takes time, however short, in which the accused had time to reflect on her actions. VO – The judge handed down her sentence. JUDGE LILLIAN VAN WYK – HIGH COURT SITTING IN PALM RIDGE – FC PROJECT This court cannot find substantial and compelling circumstances to justify a sentence less than life imprisonment. Count one, life imprisonment. Count two, life imprisonment. Count three, life imprisonment. [Cheers] LINK - FX3_1002 – The sentence may be harsh and deserved but grieving families say until they know the whole truth about what happened to their children, justice and closure remain elusive. VO – Though police say there is no evidence of a syndicate targeting children in the area, families refuse to believe that Pontsho acted alone. NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER I am not okay because I have other children. The people that Pontsho worked with will go on to kill more children. OUTRO – end with cemetery shots. PROMO 1 – 11 sec VO – Child disappearances, evil rituals, and a murderous neighbour – we investigate a series of bizarre killings that shook families in the south of Johannesburg. PROMO 2 – 21 sec VO – A young boy dies under strange circumstances but the suspect is released just months later... MORGINAH MALATJI – MPHO'S GRANDMOTHER – Then two days after her release, she took our children. VO – Families recall chilling testimony about why their childern were taken. NOMPUMELELO ZITHO – MZWANDILE'S GRANDMOTHER – They would need to sacrifice two more children, because things weren't going well for them. PROMO 3 – 21 sec VO – Dark rituals and profits - at the heart of a series of child murders... BUSISIWE MGCINA – SIMPHIWE'S MOTHER – The police did not treat us well. A lot of time passed before they helped us. VO – Despite devastating testimonies in court, residents say the area is not cursed, and blame poor policing for rampant crime. LINDA NDEBELE – COMMUNITY IN ACTION – That police station, it's a motel because they are not doing anything.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Two years after the ritual murder of three Orange Farm children, their killer is in jail, but are women & children any safer - and has the conviction restored this community's faith in the police?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: With child-killer Pontsho Mohlanka behind bars for life, the families of her little victims provide insight into how their friendly neighbour morphed into a monster to whom prosperity was more important than human life.
metadata.Summary: On the morning of the 15th of April 2020, 5-year-old Mzwandile Zitho from Orange Farm, south of Joburg, disappeared. The community joined his family in their search for the boy. His grandmother Nompumelelo reported his disappearance to the police, but on her return, neighbours confirmed her worst fears – Mzwandile was dead. He hadn’t strayed far - his body was found nearby, in a shebeen that the owner operated with his girlfriend, Pontsho Mohlanka. When Gogo Nompumelelo saw her grandson's corpse, she could scarcely believe her eyes. He was in an upright position, propped between a fridge and a counter inside the shebeen. There were strings around his neck and ankles, and a slimy black substance smeared on his body. As the occupants of the building where the body was found, Pontsho and her boyfriend were arrested on suspicion of murder. The boyfriend was released due to a lack of evidence, but Pontsho remained in custody, only to be released five months later when the charges against her were temporarily withdrawn, pending a toxicology report. Three days after her release, two more children went missing. In a scene eerily similar to the one months earlier, the bodies of Simphiwe Mgcina, 6, and Mpho Makondo, 8, were found near the shebeen, also covered in a black substance. Pontsho was rearrested. As the investigation unfolded, her boyfriend was placed in witness protection and would later testify against Pontsho. During the trial, he said she had killed the children as part of a prosperity ritual, meant to grow their tavern business. Pontsho pointed the finger at him, claiming that he was the one behind the rituals, but she failed to convince the courts. Following a month-long trial, Pontsho was found guilty of all three murders in August 2022 and will be sentenced on the 13th of September.
metadata.Further information: Orange Farm is a community plagued by violence against women and children, so much so that it has been allocated a Green Door ’safe place’ - where survivors of violence can find refuge - and their cases expedited. But residents are sceptical - they have for too long watched criminals operating without fear of the police, whom everyone believes are ineffectual. After all, they say, if the police had properly investigated Mzwandile’s murder, Pontsho’s last two victims would not have died. There are also concerns that Pontsho may not have been working alone, but acting on advice that human sacrifice would equate to prosperity. They have no faith that police will follow up and arrest others involved and doubt that ’safe places’ will change the police’s woeful investigative abilities. Whatever the various motives behind the crimes, the community believes that perpetrators commit these crimes freely, confident that the cops won't connect them. Residents also complain about a lack of visible policing in the area, despite the recent allocation of 15 additional vehicles. By focusing on this case, we will tell the story of Orange Farm’s crime scourge and why we report on the same horrific incidents, year after year and find out whether the latest initiative has any chance of success.
